t: Square Equals Product of Two Numbers - Hash the Squares, Scan the Pairs
o:
## Understanding the problem

We count triplets of two kinds: a squared element of one array equal to the product of two elements at distinct indices of the other, plus the mirrored version with the arrays swapped. Triplet identity depends on indices, so duplicate values multiply the count - with `[1,1]` and `[1,1,1]` every combination is valid and the answer is 9.

Example 1 contains exactly one match: 4^2 = 2 * 8. Example 3 finds `3^2 = 1 * 9` one way and `7^2 = 7 * 7` the other way, for a total of 2. Values reach 100000, so squares and products reach 10^10 and demand 64-bit arithmetic; lengths reach 1000, making roughly a million pair-products per direction the budget - hashing absorbs that easily while triple loops do not.
k: Reframe both types identically: count index pairs in one array whose product equals a precomputed square from the other array.
Store each square value of one array in a hash map with its multiplicity; every pair product of the other array then costs a single O(1) lookup.
Products reach 10^10, so C++ and Java need 64-bit integers to avoid overflow.

a.i: Check every (i, j, k) combination literally: for each element of one array, test all index pairs of the other and compare the square against the product. This is the definition transcribed into code and nearly impossible to get wrong, but near the length limits the roughly 10^9 comparisons are far too slow.
s: Write a helper count(a, b) that counts pairs in b whose product equals some a[i] squared.
Loop i over a; loop j < k over b.
Accumulate a match whenever a[i]*a[i] equals b[j]*b[k].
a.t: O(n*m^2 + m*n^2) - every element is paired against every pair of the other array.

a.i: Precompute a hash map from each square appearing in one array to its multiplicity. Then for every index pair j < k in the other array, a single lookup adds the number of matching squares. Work collapses to building the maps plus one linear pass over pairs, executed once in each direction.
s: Build cnt1 mapping x*x to multiplicity for x in nums1, and cnt2 symmetrically.
For each pair j < k in nums2, add cnt1[nums2[j] * nums2[k]] to the answer.
For each pair j < k in nums1, add cnt2[nums1[j] * nums1[k]].
a.t: O(n^2 + m^2) - one pass over pairs per direction with O(1) average lookups.
a.sp: O(n + m) - the two square-count hash maps.

w: Jump straight to the hashed version; deriving it from brute force takes one sentence - trade enumeration for lookup. Pitfalls: forgetting the symmetric second direction, missing the 64-bit promotion of products before comparing or hashing (a classic wrong-answer in C++ and Java), and mishandling duplicates by hand when multiplicities already cover them. Edge cases: all-equal arrays like example 2, and single-element arrays that contribute no pairs in their mirrored role. Likely follow-ups: allow negative values or zeros (hashing survives untouched), or enumerate the actual triplets instead of counting them.
